author: Henry David Thoreau
title: Walden
argument: Says people who once fed and sheltered themselves directly have become dependent on the tools and property they built, so that 'men have become the tools of their tools.'
side: yes: reliance on contrivances erodes self-provision
checked: Gutenberg #205 full text; phrase found in 'Economy' chapter.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Erewhon; or, Over the Range
argument: The Erewhonian treatise argues men already live 'in a state of bondage to the machines' and would suffer terribly if machines vanished, since they can no longer live without them.
side: yes: dependence on machines has already made people unable to live without them
checked: Gutenberg #1906; passages located in Ch. XXIV.

author: E. M. Forster
title: The Machine Stops
argument: Imagines a humanity that lives entirely inside a Machine that supplies all needs; when it fails, people cannot survive, having lost the knowledge and bodily capacity to act for themselves.
side: yes: total reliance leaves people helpless
checked: Gutenberg #72890 (The Eternal Moment and Other Stories, 1928), story text searched; first published Oxford and Cambridge Review 1909.

author: M. K. Gandhi
title: Hind Swaraj, or Indian Home Rule
argument: Argues machinery has impoverished India by destroying hand industry and that Indians should reduce their use of mills and machines and return to hand-spinning and hand-weaving.
side: yes: machine goods destroyed India's capacity to clothe itself
translation: Gandhi's own English translation, Indian Home Rule (1910); 1921 Madras edition on Internet Archive
checked: Internet Archive 1921 Natesan edition, table of contents and Ch. XIX text read.

author: Charles Babbage
title: On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures
argument: Argues that a machine which halves the time needed to make an article lets a self-supplying household enjoy the same comforts with less labour, and that displaced labour is soon reabsorbed.
side: no: machinery increases what people can provide for themselves
where: Chapter 32, "On the Effect of Machinery in Reducing the Demand for Labour"
checked: Gutenberg #4238; Chapter 32 opening paragraphs (§404) read.

author: Oscar Wilde
title: The Soul of Man under Socialism
argument: Argues that under proper social arrangements machinery will do all necessary and unpleasant work, freeing people to cultivate themselves; at present it competes with men only because of private ownership.
side: no: machines should serve man and free him
checked: Gutenberg #1017; passage 'Under proper conditions machinery will serve man' found.

author: Peter Kropotkin
title: Fields, Factories and Workshops
argument: Argues that the spread of industrial skill and intensive agriculture lets each nation and region produce its own food and manufactures instead of depending on distant specialised centres.
side: no: modern technique lets communities provide for themselves
checked: Gutenberg #64353 (1912 revised edition); Ch. I contents and text searched. First ed. 1899.

author: Mary Shelley
title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
argument: Victor, who never intended his creature to kill, judges himself 'not in deed, but in effect' the true murderer when his brother is killed and Justine condemned.
side: yes: the maker bears guilt for unintended harms
checked: Gutenberg #84 full text; quoted line located in Chapter 9.

author: Karel Čapek
title: Krakatit
argument: A chemist who invents a catastrophic explosive is pursued by those who want to use it, witnesses an explosion he did not intend, and at the end is told to give up great things and do small things that help people.
side: yes: the inventor cannot shed the burden of what his invention does
checked: Gutenberg #79127 (Hyde translation) searched; ending read. Also IA 'krakatit0000cape' (1925).

author: H. G. Wells
title: The World Set Free
argument: The physicist Holsten, frightened by the consequences of his discovery of atomic energy, feels he ought not to publish and that wise men should hold it until the world is ready.
side: yes: the discoverer feels answerable for later uses
checked: Gutenberg #1059; Holsten passage found in Chapter the First.

author: Norbert Wiener
title: A Scientist Rebels
argument: Refuses to share his wartime guided-missile research, arguing after Hiroshima that supplying scientific information is not an innocent act and that the scientist must answer for its use.
side: yes: scientists are responsible for foreseeable misuse
checked: Web search: Atlantic Monthly, January 1947; Wikipedia 'Norbert Wiener' and other secondary pages quote the letter. Full text not opened.

author: Bertrand Russell
title: Icarus, or the Future of Science
argument: Argues science only lets the holders of power realise their purposes more fully; whether it does good or harm depends on those purposes, which at present are mostly evil.
side: no: harm lies with those who wield science, not with science itself
checked: Internet Archive 'icarusorfutureof00russ' text; closing passage read (p. 57).

author: J. B. S. Haldane
title: Daedalus, or Science and the Future
argument: Uses Daedalus, who caused the death of Minos yet was never punished, to argue that the scientific worker is not concerned with gods and that mankind must adjust its morality to the powers science gives it.
side: no: the inventor's task is discovery; society must adapt its morals
checked: Internet Archive text; Daedalus passage (pp. 47–48) and closing pages read.

author: Francis Bacon
title: New Atlantis
argument: The scientists of Salomon's House consult on which of their inventions to publish and swear an oath to keep secret those they think fit, revealing some only to the state.
side: yes: dangerous inventions should be withheld by those who make them
checked: Gutenberg #2434; oath-of-secrecy passage read. Published posthumously 1626/1627.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Darwin among the Machines
argument: Signed 'Cellarius', the letter argues machines are evolving toward supremacy over man and that 'war to the death' should be proclaimed and every machine destroyed.
side: yes: destroy machines before they escape control
checked: Reprinted in A First Year in Canterbury Settlement, with Other Early Essays (1914), IA text read; note says it appeared in the Christchurch Press, 13 June 1863. Tone partly satirical.

author: Zhuangzi
title: Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu), 'Heaven and Earth'
argument: A gardener refuses a well-sweep that would water a hundred times more ground, saying that cunning implements produce cunning hearts unfit for the Tao.
side: yes: refuse a useful device because of its effect on the user
translation: Herbert A. Giles, Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer (1889); Gutenberg #59709
checked: Gutenberg #59709; passage read in Giles's Chapter XII. Year given is the translation; original c. 4th–3rd c. BCE.

author: Plenipotentiaries of the Hague Peace Conference
title: Declaration concerning Asphyxiating Gases (Hague Declaration IV, 2)
argument: The contracting powers agree to abstain from projectiles whose object is the diffusion of asphyxiating or deleterious gases.
side: yes: ban a weapon technology in advance
translation: Official English text on Avalon Project
checked: Avalon Project (Yale) text read.

author: J. B. S. Haldane
title: Callinicus: A Defence of Chemical Warfare
argument: Argues gas weapons such as tear gas are more humane than shells and bayonets, and that the Hague ban on gas projectiles was well meant but misguided.
side: no: restricting the invention does more harm than using it
checked: Internet Archive text; Hague and 'most humane weapon' passages read.

author: Andrew Ure
title: The Philosophy of Manufactures
argument: Defends self-acting machinery against the charge that it harasses the poor, arguing that the blessings of mechanical science to society have been too little recognised.
side: no: machinery's benefits outweigh its alleged harms
checked: Internet Archive 1835 edition text; 'blessings which physico-mechanical science has bestowed' passage read.

author: Jeremy Bentham
title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
argument: Argues that what matters for moral standing is not whether a being can reason or talk but whether it can suffer.
side: yes: capacity to suffer grounds a claim
checked: Internet Archive 1907 Clarendon edition text; 'Can they suffer?' found in Ch. XVII.

author: Voltaire
title: Philosophical Dictionary, 'Animals'
argument: Attacks the Cartesian view of animals as machines: a dog dissected alive has all the organs of feeling, and nature did not give it nerves in order that it should not feel.
side: yes: organs of feeling show animals suffer, so vivisection is barbarous
checked: Gutenberg #18569 English text; passage read.

author: Thomas Henry Huxley
title: On the Hypothesis that Animals are Automata, and Its History
argument: Holds animals may be conscious automata; because they probably feel and an error could have terrible consequences, they should be treated as weaker brethren.
side: yes: possible suffering in a mechanism warrants humane treatment
checked: Collected in Method and Results (1893), Internet Archive text; closing passage read.

author: Henry S. Salt
title: Animals' Rights Considered in Relation to Social Progress
argument: Argues that if men have rights so do the lower animals, and rejects doctrines that deny animals feel pain.
side: yes: sentient beings have rights
where: Chapter I, "The Principle of Animals' Rights"
checked: Gutenberg #64498; Chapter I heading and text read.

author: Mary Shelley
title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
argument: The creature demands that his maker relieve his misery, arguing that he was benevolent until suffering made him a fiend.
side: yes: an artificial being's suffering creates obligations
checked: Gutenberg #84; 'Remember that I am thy creature' passage in Chapter 10.

author: Karel Čapek
title: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)
argument: Dr Gall adds pain nerves to the Robots only so they will not damage themselves; asked if they will be happier, he says no, only more perfect technically, while Helena's Humanity League campaigns for them.
side: both: pain engineered as a technical feature versus a claim to humane treatment
translation: Paul Selver and Nigel Playfair (1923); Gutenberg #59112
checked: Gutenberg #59112; pain-nerves dialogue and Humanity League lines read in Act One.

author: René Descartes
title: Discourse on the Method
argument: Argues animals are machines made by God whose actions follow from the disposition of their organs, and that they lack reason and a rational soul.
side: no: animals are automata without minds
checked: Gutenberg #59; Part V read. Descartes does not state here that animals cannot feel; Huxley's 1874 essay reports later Cartesians taking that view.

author: John Locke
title: Second Treatise of Government
argument: Argues men are God's property because they are his workmanship, but that human parents do not own children they beget, since children are the workmanship of their maker, the Almighty.
side: both: only the true maker owns; human begetters have duties, not ownership
checked: Gutenberg #7370; §6 and §56 read.

author: Robert Filmer
title: Patriarcha: or, the Natural Power of Kings
argument: Argues Adam and the patriarchs held absolute power of life and death over their families by natural right of fatherhood.
side: yes: begetting gives dominion
checked: Internet Archive 1680 edition text; passage read before 'CHAP. II'.

author: Thomas Hobbes
title: Leviathan
argument: Argues a parent's dominion over a child does not derive from having begotten it but from the child's consent.
side: no: making does not create a right of dominion
where: Chapter XX, "Of Dominion Paternall and Despoticall"
checked: Gutenberg #3207; Chapter XX passage read.

author: Aristotle
title: Politics
argument: Calls a slave an animated instrument and property, and says that if tools could work of themselves, like the statues of Daedalus, masters would not need slaves.
side: yes: a living instrument is property of its master
checked: Gutenberg #6762; passage read. Year given is the Ellis translation.

author: Mary Shelley
title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
argument: The creature tells Victor 'I ought to be thy Adam', and Victor recognises 'the duties of a creator towards his creature', framing the relation as obligation rather than ownership.
side: no: the maker owes duties to what he makes
checked: Gutenberg #84; both lines located in Chapter 10.

author: Karel Čapek
title: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)
argument: Robots are manufactured and sold by a company as products; the play ends with their revolt against their makers.
side: both: makers treat creations as property; the creations reject it
translation: Paul Selver and Nigel Playfair (1923); Gutenberg #59112
checked: Gutenberg #59112 searched.

author: Auguste Villiers de l'Isle-Adam
title: The Future Eve
argument: A fictional Edison builds an artificial woman, Hadaly, and gives her to Lord Ewald as a replacement for the woman he loves.
side: yes: the made being is a possession to be bestowed
checked: French Wikisource text exists; English Wikipedia summary. Plot recalled, not re-read.

author: Francis Bacon
title: Novum Organum
argument: Says man lost both his innocence and his dominion over creation at the Fall; religion can restore the first and the arts and sciences the second.
side: yes: invention recovers a God-given dominion
checked: Gutenberg #45988; passage found in Book II, Aphorism LII.

author: Walt Whitman
title: Passage to India
argument: Celebrates the Suez Canal, the transcontinental railroad and the Atlantic cable as fulfilling God's original purpose of linking the earth, after which the poet will justify the inventors.
side: yes: engineering works carry out divine intent
checked: Internet Archive, Two Rivulets (1876) reprint; stanza on 'the first intent' and 'noble inventors' read.

author: Henri de Saint-Simon
title: New Christianity
argument: Argues God's command that men treat each other as brothers now requires directing the sciences, arts and industry to the fastest improvement of the poorest class.
side: yes: industry and science are the means of fulfilling the divine command
checked: Internet Archive 1825 edition text searched ('Dieu a dit', 'classe la plus pauvre').

author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
title: The Celestial Railroad
argument: Satire in which a railroad promises to carry pilgrims to the Celestial City without toil, but the line ends at the gates of hell.
side: no: mechanical conveniences counterfeit spiritual progress
checked: Gutenberg #512 (Mosses from an Old Manse), story located.

author: J. B. S. Haldane
title: Daedalus, or Science and the Future
argument: Says every physical or chemical invention has been hailed as an insult to some god and every biological invention as a perversion; the inventor is always a Prometheus.
side: no: invention defies the gods rather than serving them
checked: Internet Archive text; Prometheus passage read.

author: Thomas Carlyle
title: Signs of the Times
argument: Calls the age mechanical in head and heart; men hope only in mechanism, and worship an idol of Strength instead of the Beautiful and Good.
side: yes: faith in mechanism displaces worship
checked: Internet Archive text (Edinburgh Review, June 1829); 'faith', 'worship' and 'idol' passages read.

author: Matthew Arnold
title: Culture and Anarchy
argument: Says 'faith in machinery' is England's besetting danger: freedom, coal, railroads, wealth and even religious organisations are treated as ends in themselves.
side: yes: machinery is valued as if it were an end
checked: Gutenberg #4212; passage read in Chapter I.

author: Henry Adams
title: The Education of Henry Adams
argument: At the 1900 Paris Exposition Adams feels the dynamos as a moral force, as early Christians felt the Cross, and finds himself inclined to pray to one.
side: yes: the dynamo becomes an object of worship
where: Chapter XXV, "The Dynamo and the Virgin (1900)"
checked: Gutenberg #2044; Chapter XXV read. Privately printed 1907, published 1918.

author: E. M. Forster
title: The Machine Stops
argument: People consult the Book of the Machine as scripture and come to worship the Machine that serves them.
side: yes: dependence becomes worship
checked: Gutenberg #72890; 'worship the Machine' passages found.

author: Edward Carpenter
title: Civilisation: Its Cause and Cure
argument: Says locomotives, machinery and telegraphs must be reduced to subjection to the real man instead of remaining objects of 'mere fetish-worship as now'.
side: yes: machinery is currently a fetish
checked: Gutenberg #44094; passage read in Section IV.

author: Nikolai Berdyaev
title: Man and Machine
argument: Argues modern civilisation puts tools in the place of their users and that, without a spiritual reorientation, technology will destroy man as a person.
side: yes: technology usurps man's spiritual place
translation: No public-domain English translation; English translation in Technology and Language (2023)
checked: Web search: published in the émigré journal Put' (Paris), 1933; soctech.spbstu.ru English translation page.

author: Timothy Walker
title: Defence of Mechanical Philosophy
argument: Reply to Carlyle's 'Signs of the Times' defending mechanical invention as freeing people from drudgery for higher pursuits.
side: no: mechanism serves the mind, it is not a false faith
checked: Web search: North American Review 33, no. 72 (July 1831): 122–136 (JSTOR 25102907). Full text not opened; argument summarised from catalogue descriptions.

author: Lewis Henry Morgan
title: Ancient Society
argument: Divides human history into savagery, barbarism and civilization, marking the stages largely by a sequence of inventions and discoveries.
side: yes: technical invention measures the ascent to civilization
where: Part I, "Growth of Intelligence through Inventions and Discoveries"
checked: Gutenberg #45950; Part I heading and preface read.

author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
title: Lord Bacon
argument: Judges Bacon's philosophy by its fruits: it has lengthened life, spanned rivers, annihilated distance and driven cars without horses; its law is progress.
side: yes: mechanical achievement is the mark of advancement
checked: Gutenberg #2333 (Critical and Historical Essays, vol. 2); essay dated July 1837 (Edinburgh Review); passage read.

author: M. K. Gandhi
title: Hind Swaraj, or Indian Home Rule
argument: Argues modern civilization, whose chief symbol is machinery, is an irreligious condition; true civilization is moral conduct, and India's ancestors chose not to pursue machinery.
side: no: machinery is a mark of false civilization
where: Chapter VI, "Civilisation"; Chapter XIII, "What is True Civilisation?"
translation: Gandhi's own English translation, Indian Home Rule (1910); 1921 Madras edition on Internet Archive
checked: Internet Archive 1921 edition; table of contents and chapter text read.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
title: Nationalism
argument: Argues the West has turned society into a machine of commerce and politics whose aim is success, not goodness, eliminating moral responsibility.
side: no: mechanical organisation is not moral progress
checked: Gutenberg #40766; passage in 'Nationalism in the West' read.

author: Oswald Spengler
title: Man and Technics
argument: Treats machine technology as the expression of Western man's will to power, a stage in a culture's life that ends in decline.
side: no: machinery marks a late, declining phase
translation: C. T. Atkinson (1932); public-domain status not verified
checked: English Wikipedia summary (1931 book; will-to-power reading). Text not opened.

author: Charles Babbage
title: On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures
argument: Says a country must have reached a high degree of civilization before it approaches the limit of economy in applying force to transport.
side: yes: mechanical economy advances with civilization
checked: Gutenberg #4238; §19 read. §19 falls in Chapter 1.
